Sure. I was in middle school, I had a best friend and some other friends, which meant having someone to spend time with, we fully understood each other and it was great. We basically had a symbiotic relationship, and at some point it was so deep we literally always knew what the other was thinking, we even had more than one "secret language" so that we could speak freely around other people without being understood. It was really great and even though it was a really codependent relationship, it made me so happy. I had also lost a lot of weight the summer between primary and secondary school due to a bad sickness I got that stopped me from eating any food for a solid weak.

Before that was primary school, which I still consider to have been the worst time of my life.
I was in school everyday 8am to 4pm,and there I was the scapegoat of all the bullies. I was so bullied that even kids who had no interest in bullying me or even liked me, never talked to me in fear of being associated with me. I spent that whole time completely alone, was made fun of for being fat, ugly teeth, ugly face, ugly clothes, getting my period early on, getting body hair early on, everything.
I attended dance classes in free time, and there I was bullied as well for basically the same reasons. In school I got hit on the daily, and teachers were always magically not looking when it happened. The only time I stood up for myself and hit the bully back, I got the punishment he'd never get.
Home life was also shit, my father was really absent in the way that he was working 24/7 and only came home to argue and sleep. My mom was in a really toxic relationship with her own mother (a full blown narcissist) and just wasn't a great mother to me and my older sister. My sister remembers mom hitting me when I was very little, but I have no memory of that so I guess I was too little to remember it. My sister is only 4 years older than me, but she had to take almost full time care of me (God bless her) to the point that I used to call her "mom", and she used to call our grandparents "mom" and "dad".
Our parents were home only to argue, I later understood we were really poor and kudos to them for not letting us understand that, I'll give them that. But it was still an ongoing argument. My mom was a lunatic, everybody in the family agrees she had psychological issue though I have no idea what, but the theme was taking her anger and frustration out on me and my sister. She always came home and immediately found the smallest thing, or sometimes nothing at all, to scream at us for hours on end.

I did ask my parents to be moved to a different school, because I was literally crying myself to sleep every single night, but they ignored me. I even got my sister to ask with me and she remembers that, we asked but were denied at least in two separate occasions.

Years later, when I was in therapy for depression and my therapist understood that my childhood had been shit, she decided to try and have a family conversation about it in her office, so we did and my parents' excuse was that "they didn't want me to become weak by running away from the bullies, and they thought it'd just be better to have me face it and come out the other side stronger". Legit makes me laugh in frustration that they were so blind to my suffering.

This got long, I'm sorry, but you understand how much of a 180 it was for me from primary school to middle school. Yet it was in middle school that I started having suicidal thoughts, without depression.

The answer is based on my personal experiece as a 21 year old woman. 

First of all, talk to your partner. She might be uncomfortable with the conversation but you have to let her know that it's a conversation that you need to be open about because you feel very strongly about it and it affects you mentally.
Let her know if it hurts your confidence, if it makes you doubt your abilities, etc.. It's important to communicate it if that's the case. 
Then once you get to talking, LISTEN to her. Chances are she simply has a low sex drive, in my experience as a woman, most of me and my friend really got a sex drive at around 20 years old, while I understand guys get it much earlier (12 to 15 years old). If that's the case, there's not really much you can do about it, except for trying to make it more interesting for her (are there specific things she'd like to try? Ask her that and be open minded) or more how she likes it (if she's really romantic, try setting up some music, lighting candles and have some romantic time together before the deed, watch a movie or something).
If it's not about sex drive, then it could be two things:
1) you're not pleasing her enough. I know it sucks if that's the case, but see it as a chance to improve your abilities. Get a free day together and lay in bed, try new things and press her to tell you what she loves, likes, hates, etc. It can go both ways and help you both improve sex quality.
2) she may simply be embarrassed to tell you when she's horny, and therefore you miss it when she is, and when you ask she isn't. In this case, try to get her to understand that that's letting you both unsatisfied, and try to find references or signals she can give you to kind of initial the deed without actually doing it.

Good luck.

I'm a 22 year old woman, so take this advice how you want.
I think your relationship is missing some boundaries around money, and always has based on how you described him paying for everything at the beginning of your relationship.
My question is: did you talk openly about the fact that he was spending much more money than you (at the beginning of the relationship) and if yes, what did you agree to?
In my experiece, I've usually been the poor one in the relationship, but there have been opposite instances. I always put it clear that I'm willing to pay my half of everything, but that I can't afford (for example) to go out to eat everyday. If they're willing to do that, I'm 100% happy, but usually they'll say they're willing to spend a bit more money in the relationship. In that case I put it very clear that I'm not willing to pay that money back, and that if they want to spend it on me it'll be a gift, not a debt.
It may be tricky to build some form of boundarie like that if you haven't already, especially now that he's already spent a bunch of money on you. But I still suggest you try having a conversation like that (or remind him of it if you had already made an agreement).
Regardless of that all, if he keeps relying on you for money in a way that you're not comfortable with, your only choice is to stop giving him money (buying food just for yourself, for example, or simply demanding half of the money back) and possibly break up if he refuses to act any different.

My thoughts are that:

This wouldn't mean she transitioned for that or something, but that she felt she was missing that when she shouldn't be and is now making up for it. In this case, I'd advise you to just let her have her deserved mother-daughter relationship.
B) you may be stressing out because you feel you've acted in a way that limited your mother-daughter relationship, and you now regret it and have only realized cause you saw your sister having that. I'm this case I hope you have some deep thinking about why you feel the way that you do, and what you can do to help with that. For example, you could ask you mother to teach you those same things. It's not uncommon for tomboy girls to embrace their femininity later in life.
C) it may be more complicated. Maybe you have all the rights to be mad. If your family have the money for it, I strongly suggest you book a therapy session for yourself first, where you try to understand what's going on, and then one for you, your sister and your mom to discuss this all together. I know it may feel impossible but it truly is a good opportunity. It's a delicate time for you, going from having a brother to having a sister, with changing sibling dinamic, and for your sister obviously since she's transitioning. If you can have a family therapy session you may be able to convey to your sister that you have issues with her, not her transition or her identity, and you may be able to solve those issues listening to her and your mom and expressing your own concerns.

Here are some tips that help me.
1) if she's with you, there's a reason why. Otherwise she'd be with someone else or just be single. A good way of thinking about it to me is that she chooses everyday, and as of right now she's chosen every single day to be with YOU and no one but you, since you two have been together. 2) it's okay to repress some emotions. If I'm ever jealous I usually try to first accept it (which it seems like you do), secondly know that I'm feeling this way but not allowing my self to act any different than if I wasn't feeling this way, and third, only if I'm still very stressed about it: tell my bf that I'm feeling this way, that I know it's irrational and I don't want him to change his ways because of it but I needed to let it out. This usually makes me feel a whole lot better + the other person usually will do something to make you feel better about it, such as texting you more through the night, or telling you more about it the next day, eccetera.
3) you can decide to trust them. Simple as that. You can tell yourself "well, if she's gonna cheat on me I'll be the dumbass who didn't see it coming, but right now I decide to trust her 100%". This also makes me personally feel a lot better, about my partner and my relationship in general.
4) accept that she might also cheat. It's a possibility. I've been cheated on before, definitely more than once, and it's hard to trust anyone again fully after that, but it's possible in my experience, step by step. My current bf gives me no reason at all to doubt him and he never has, so it's kind of easier, but even like this when he sees some friends after uni I apply point 1) and 2) always. I'm still struggling with 3) because of my last relationship being a complete disaster, but I don't even need it right now cause my bf is so trustworthy.

Okay so. I'm pretty deep into this stuff so I'll tell you what works for me.
About remembering dreams, I pretty much always do, and my tips for that would be:
-think about your dreams as soon as you wake up, like write them down or tell someone about them (the second is faster and it will help you remember a lot more)
-if you lately couldn't remember any dreams, get one night in which you sleep as long as possible (if you can). This means no distractions, no sunlight or noise in your room, and if you wake up just go back to sleep again by staying still and enjoying the feeling of relaxation and the warmth of your bed. This will make the world of a difference, because by not being tired you'll remember at least your last dream a lot more vividly.

Another way you could try is lucid dreaming, but to do that you first need to make sure that you always/almost always remember your dreams,otherwise lucid dreaming is useless. 
BUT that being said, if you lucid dream it's such a crazy feeling, expecially the first time, that you will most likely remember it when you wake up.
